speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I join the hon Members who spoke before me to congratulate you on your election as Speaker and wish you well in the discharge of your solemn duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also have some sympathy for the hon Member for Sembawang, Mr Vikram Nair, and the hon Member for Aljunied, Ms Sylvia Lim, because they were balloted out of the right to speak on this Adjournment Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I know the feeling because I was balloted out of the right to speak on this topic last month.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I go on to my speech, let me declare my interest as a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to address this House today on the following matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Courts have often found it challenging to impose sentences on offenders diagnosed with psychiatric conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst, generally, the need for rehabilitation is a key consideration for mentally disordered persons, it has to be balanced against the countervailing need for retribution and deterrence at the same time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The 2010 amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code to expand the community-based sentencing regime was a milestone in strengthening rehabilitation as an option for offenders in right cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As explained by the hon Minister of Law in this House in 2010, community-based sentencing gives more flexibility to the Courts in deciding an appropriate sentence for the offender in question.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not every offender should be put in prison.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Community-based sentencing targets offenders traditionally viewed by the Courts to be on the rehabilitation end of the spectrum, such as persons with specific and relatively minor mental conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For such cases, it is appropriate to harness the resources of the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have come to know of one such offender professionally through a Court-assigned pro bono case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Tan is a middle-aged man who has low intelligence quotient (IQ) and a gaming addiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His mother, a hawker centre cleaner, looks after him and his younger sister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was charged with the offence of stealing coins from a vending machine to feed his gaming addiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He has similar theft convictions in the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He underwent psychiatric evaluation to determine the suitability of a mandatory treatment order and was assessed as suffering from anti-social personality disorder.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, it would be contemplated that he would have to be put in sheltered care or be enrolled in pro-social programmes like anger and stress management.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To give Members of this House a sense of how such patients need to be managed, please allow me to quote the following excerpt from the United Kingdom (UK) Code of Practice for the Mental Health Act: "Generally, treatment approaches for personality disorder need to be relatively intense and long-term, structured and coherent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sustainable long-term change is more likely to be achieved with the voluntary engagement of the patient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: People with personality disorders may take time to engage and develop motivation for such longer-term treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But even patients who are not engaged in that kind of treatment may need other forms of treatment, including nurse and specialist care, to manage the continuing risks posed by their disorders." So, we see, they need significantly more than just psychiatric help.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the Court, under the current Criminal Procedure Code provisions, was unable to consider imposing an MTO in the event a psychiatrist does not support it, it proceeded to consider Mr Tan's suitability for conditional discharge under the Probation of Offenders Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we explored here was his voluntary participation in a programme that was put up with community support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This programme would have allowed him to be economically active and engaged with the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the assistance of Bizlink, a voluntary welfare organisation (VWO), and a counsellor with the Marine Parade Family Service Centre, Mr Tan started learning how to work for the first time in his life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, due to the influence of some others, he started re-offending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He dismantled a bicycle wheel from a bicycle and stole it, leaving the bicycle behind, as a favour to a friend.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Later, he punched a person in his face for intervening in a quarrel between him and his mother at a hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not the end of the matter for his family.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His sister also suffers from a psychiatric condition and was a co-accused in one of the offences Mr Tan committed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She needs help before her situation becomes as serious as her brother's.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst our current regime allows for community sentencing, such as an MTO for offenders with mental disorders, this is predicated on the offender being assessed to be suitable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When a guarded prognosis is given, it does not mean that the offender's treatment is not treatable at all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What it usually means is that the psychiatric treatment alone is unlikely to lead to the changes necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, though, the main sentencing option for such offenders with guarded prognosis is a jail term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sending such offenders to jail, in my respectful view, is not an ideal solution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The chances of such offenders reoffending are great.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, such offenders are often victims of their circumstance, vulnerable to influence by people with bad intentions, and are often persuaded to do things which would get them into even more trouble, as was the case for Mr Tan.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the very least, it would be in the interest of the general public to manage an offender's condition through a networked approach so as to ensure that his condition that led to his offending behaviour does not worsen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that, in prison, only offenders with Axis 1 mental disorders are provided treatment, but not Axis 2 disorders, beyond, at times, administering some medication to calm them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Axis 1 disorders are the more familiar ones, such as depression or schizophrenia, whereas Axis 2 disorders are usually lifelong problems, such as anti-social personality disorder, paranoid personality disorder and mental retardation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The lack of treatment for or appropriate management of the psychiatric condition of such offenders would mean that they may exit prisons without the additional social and emotional skills to manage life, with the result that the risk of re-offending is not lessened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Examples of other sentencing options for such offenders may include mandatory in-patient treatment whilst serving a jail term, and mandatory regular reporting to a prescribed officer for monitoring even after the prison sentence has been served.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such options have been implemented in the UK vis-a-vis Axis 2 disorders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There, besides a hospital order, which is similar to our MTO, the courts there have the option of making a hybrid order where an offender is sentenced to a period of imprisonment and is simultaneously admitted to hospital for a period of treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, the UK courts have the ability to make a restriction order over and above the hybrid order or the hospital order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2008, the "appropriate treatment test" was introduced to replace the old test. "Treatment" is defined as including nursing, psychological intervention and specialist mental health rehabilitation and care.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Treatment includes anything from a cure to containment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The new test allows the court to make a detention order for treatment so long as, having regard to the nature and degree of the mental disorder and all other circumstances, the "appropriate medical treatment is available to him".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Arising from the above, in the UK, they have multidisciplinary teams that assess more holistic sentencing options for the courts, not just psychiatric treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If such an approach is adopted in Singapore, admittedly, there would be a need to enhance the resources committed for community-based sentencing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hopefully, the Government will be able to rely on VWO support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, with respect to offenders who do have independent means of support, perhaps it may not be necessary for the psychiatric treatment component of MTOs to be administered via the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), which would involve public resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, private sector resources can be drawn in, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In short, the options that I have identified, in my view, will allow judges to have more discretion to impose bespoke sentences on offenders suffering from serious mental conditions, especially personality disorders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also believe such an approach, in the long run, better serves the public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Separately, I have seen situations where conditional warnings were given in lieu of prosecution to mentally disordered offenders, especially youthful offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister of Law explained in 2010 that conditional warnings are part and parcel of prosecutorial discretion and does not need to be hard coded in our laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a parallel, I wish to highlight the multidisciplinary approach taken by the Community Court, in certain cases, through the Community Court Conference (CCC) prior to sentencing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had the privilege of personally witnessing the efficacy of this approach in one case involving a 15-year-old boy in Bukit Batok who was given a warning in lieu of prosecution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This boy was diagnosed with autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and also suffers from a gaming addiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Despite his young age, he has gotten into trouble with the law quite a few times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, he was arrested for being in possession of a dangerous weapon.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, through the instigation of some negative influences, he posted a video of himself on the Internet deriding a particular gang.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His father petitioned the Police not to charge him in Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Police agreed and administered his son with a stern warning instead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, the boy continued to cause disruption not just within his family but in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His father tearfully recounted that his son, for the first time, started laying his hands on him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To help the boy and his family, community leaders, the family social worker, his school teachers, psychiatrist, psychologist and the Police formed a social network to support him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I met these representatives with a view to coordinate their efforts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this approach, this boy is now required to regularly report to officers at a Neighbourhood Police Post.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Operators of the gaming arcades in the vicinity were advised not to allow him in, should he visit them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His school teachers would check periodically to see if the boy takes his medication, which, unfortunately, is not a given.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His psychiatrist has made some adjustments to his medication regime so that the monitoring could be done more easily.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The community leaders continue to provide support to the family and continue to keep an eye on him with a view to keep him out of harm's way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current situation of enforcement authorities imposing conditions on the mentally disordered offender for not prosecuting him would not provide sufficient assurance against him re-offending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a need to bring in the relevant agencies, work out a programme and monitor the progress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Often, the offender's family alone is simply unable to cope, especially a broken family.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The challenge, though, is to identify the right Government agency to lead and manage this initiative because we are looking at a broad spectrum of matters − enforcement of law, treatment, rehabilitation and drawing on VWO and community resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, it may be appropriate for an inter-Ministerial panel to be set up to look into this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I strongly believe that Mr Tan's sister would have benefited from participating in such a programme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She received an unconditional warning from the Police for her participation in the theft case with her brother.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately for her, she is not put into any rehabilitative programme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another area of sentencing, which I respectfully suggest the Minister also review, is the applicability of community sentences for offences that stipulate mandatory or specified minimum sentences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Law, in a reply dated 8 May 2017, stated that the Ministry does not intend to do so as these offences are seen as more serious.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, I do not see how it can be safely assumed that just because Parliament provides a specified minimum or mandatory sentence, it must mean that Parliament considers this offence to be so serious as to be excluded from community-based sentencing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, in a Straits Times article dated 28 March 2017, a man was reported to have received a short detention order, a form of community sentence, for filming women in bathrooms, which is an offence of insulting the modesty of a woman under section 509 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, a first-time offender convicted for an offence of possessing uncensored films under section 21 of the Films Act would be ineligible for community sentencing because that Act prescribes a fine of not less than $100 for each such film in the offender's possession.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, in drink driving cases under section 67 of the Road Traffic Act where injury or damage is caused and the custody threshold is breached, community sentencing is not available because the Road Traffic Act prescribes a minimum fine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Comparatively, in a Straits Times article dated 14 July 2016, it was reported that a motorist charged with causing death by a negligent act under section 304A of the Penal code was given a community sentence, a short detention order, as that section of the Penal Code did not prescribe a mandatory sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These anomalies were also highlighted by a specially convened High Court Bench consisting of three judges in a 2015 case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The High Court stated that while Parliament decides on the relative gravity of offences, the policy considerations that underlie a legislative choice to impose a mandatory or specified minimum sentence may not necessarily be identical or relevant to the consideration of whether or not probation should be given or available in a particular case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, and I quote, "Each society seeks to strike a balance between the rights of society to secure conviction of a person who commits an offence and the rights of an individual… I will freely admit that there can be reasonable debate as to whether that balance has been rightly struck...

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The procedure to be adopted for administration of criminal justice is an area where there are diverse and often contentious viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is an evolutionary process and we will have to continue to be open to amending our criminal procedures to meet changing norms".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is correct to take an evolutionary approach as we must be mindful of unintended consequences of effecting change in our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In many other societies, mentally disordered persons continue to be stigmatised and shunned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The typical sentencing solution for mentally disordered offenders with serious conditions is to segregate and keep them away as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even in Singapore, if we do not effect a change in legislative policy, Mr Tan and people like him will eventually run the danger of being imposed corrective training and preventive detention in prison.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In layman terms, it means locking them up for long periods of time without the possibility of remission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This continues to be celebrated in the criminal bar as a major turning point in relation to sentencing policy of especially mentally disordered offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However difficult the journey may be, we must show that we are with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In principle, the Government shares the same objectives as Mr Murali.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have been moving in the direction of extending more rehabilitative options to those who commit offences, especially those who suffer from mental health conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Community-Based Sentencing (CBS) scheme was introduced in the CPC in 2010 to harness the resources of the community in rehabilitating offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Each year, the Courts have been making about 80 MTOs, which are targeted at persons with mental health conditions; and 80 Community Service Orders (CSOs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have seen encouraging results on both these schemes, and I have been told that some who complete their CSOs even continue to volunteer with the organisation where they served their sentence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We can go further, and intend to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For offenders with mental health conditions in particular, we are proposing to expand the range of offences that are eligible for MTOs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some crimes may be too serious and it would not serve the justice system well to allow the offenders to be on the CBS regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, the regime has to be carefully calibrated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will need to draw a line somewhere, even if that means that some will fall outside the regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to examine the eligibility requirements and extend the line where appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This brings me to Mr Murali's point relating to the availability of CBS for offences with mandatory minimum or specified minimum sentences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One area where we think the line should be drawn is where mandatory minimum sentences are concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such sentences are only prescribed for very serious offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Murali's other point relates to the availability of treatment for offenders whose mental health conditions have been clinically assessed as being not susceptible to treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are good reasons why these offenders are not given MTOs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It would pose a danger to the public and undermine confidence in our criminal justice system if offenders who would otherwise be imprisoned are allowed to remain in the community, even though there is no prospect that the underlying cause of their offending can be addressed through medical treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This does not mean that these offenders are not given treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I understand that all inmates diagnosed with mental health conditions are seen regularly by prison psychiatrists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a large spectrum of such conditions, and the medical professionals will decide on the degree of treatment and management required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Singapore Prison Service also works closely with IMH and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) to ensure continuity in monitoring and treating inmates with mental health conditions once they are released.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, inmates whose conditions are unstable will be escorted to IMH upon their release, for continued treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IMH also makes arrangements for those requiring outpatient psychiatric treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For those who may not be able to return home, the Singapore Prison Service works with VWOs, such as the Singapore Association for Mental Health, to emplace them in special care homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We regularly examine our practices and systems to ensure that the best possible measures are in place to give these offenders their best shot at effective rehabilitation, subject to what is feasible, given available resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will carefully study Mr Murali's comments, including the UK approach he has referred to, to ensure as much as possible that nobody falls through the cracks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These strategies often entail close cooperation between various Government agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our Police Force works with multiple stakeholders, including the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), the Family Service Centres and IMH, to achieve this objective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where an Investigation Officer assesses that there are relevant issues through the course of investigation, such as underlying mental or socio-familial issues, a referral will be made to the appropriate agency for their follow-up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Community Policing Unit also engages community groups regularly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where appropriate, they are able to render support to reduce re-offending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are also a number of programmes available to persons with mental health conditions who are at risk of committing offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, IMH's "Response, Early Intervention, Assessment in Community mental Health" teams (REACH) have been working with school counsellors to assist students with psychological, emotional and behavioural problems, including students with addictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Interventions are provided within the student's school or, if necessary, at the IMH Child Guidance Clinic (CGC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Children and youths who have committed offences and are suspected to have underlying mental health conditions, may be referred from the Police or MSF to IMH's "Forensic Rehabilitation, Intervention, Evaluation and Network Development Service" (FRIENDS) team.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The FRIENDS team will provide assessment and treatment, including group therapy and home visits, and work with community resources to support these youths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I hope that family and friends, VWOs and other community leaders can continue to work together to support the rehabilitation of these persons.
